text: A playbook never decides on its own when to run. Lesson 25 covered what a playbook actually is — a real Azure Logic App with a Microsoft Sentinel connector trigger. But out of every incident Sentinel creates, deciding which ones actually reach that trigger is a separate job, handled by a separate Sentinel object: the automation rule.

The automation rule decides when an action happens. The playbook decides what that action actually does. Keeping those two decisions in two separate objects is what makes the whole system composable instead of one tangled special case for every scenario you'll ever automate.

An automation rule fires on one of two real trigger types. When incident is created fires once, at the exact moment Sentinel creates a new incident — the natural moment to kick off a first response. When incident is updated fires every time an existing incident changes, so a rule can react mid-investigation, say the moment severity gets manually escalated to High.

A trigger alone would fire on every single incident, so rules add conditions — if/then logic evaluated against the incident's properties, like severity, title, analytics rule name, or tags. Put a trigger and a condition together and you get a full automation rule in one sentence: when an incident is created, and its severity is High, run this playbook.

A rule's action is only one thing it can do. Beyond running a playbook, the same rule can tag an incident, assign an owner, or change its status, and it can chain more than one action together. Because the rule holds the condition and not the playbook, you can point the identical playbook at a phishing rule and a brute-force rule without rebuilding the workflow twice.

Rule decides when, playbook decides what — and separating them is what lets one workflow serve several different scenarios. Next: a full worked example, start to finish, watching a real phishing incident trigger a rule that runs a playbook.
